findings.text: the drain view's stuck rule is now `stuck = bool(overdue and last_verdict)` with no filter on the pointer's phase or on the verdict word, so any live pointer older than an hour that has any recorded verdict lands in view['stuck']; before this change only phase queued/launch-failed (and an awaiting-upstream whose waits would resolve) counted. Runs.drain builds `pointers` from list_live (reckon/crew/runs.py:2282) and a pass writes verdict="launched" for a request it launched (reckon/crew/queue_admission.py:4072), so a dispatch that has been working for over an hour now reads as stuck. The plan asked the view to read the recorded STALL verdict in place of resolving waits, not any verdict.

the done-when's second bullet — "the drain view reports its age" — is asserted by no test: the four tests in tests/test_the_queue_reports_its_own_stalls.py exercise queue_admission.admit_once and needs_you.needs_you_rows only, and neither they nor any other test calls runs._drain_week_view or runs.drain for the new admissible_age_seconds, age_seconds, stalled, stage and stage_seconds fields; the whole drain-view half of the landed change, including the stuck-rule replacement, is unmeasured, and the defect above passed because of it.

test_old_upstream_wait_is_stuck_only_when_admission_would_advance_it still passes but no longer guards the rule it names: it asserts resolve_waits separately (:180-:197) and then reads the stuck list, which the landed change derives from recorded verdicts rather than from resolve_waits; r-waiting has no verdict in its fixture (:198-:208) so it is absent from the stuck list for a reason the test does not state, and it would now be stuck if one were recorded. The test reads as coverage of the retired rule and gives none.

`stalled[0]["stage"] == recorded[0]["stage"]` is a round-trip assertion: the test writes the value the writer produced (recorded[0], from _admit) into the verdict log at :164 and then compares the reader's output against that same variable, so it holds whatever stage the writer records and would survive the writer regressing; the kinds of row the assertion does guard independently are len(stalled)==1, kind=="blocked" and the age bound at :169.

_stall_verdicts re-implements the verdict-log read the landed change also adds inline in runs._drain_week_view (:2111-:2145) and in queue_admission._last_verdict_of (): all three parse the same lines, keep the last verdict per run and track the stall fields, so the stall/clear semantics now live in three places; no shared reader existed before the change, and one could have been added rather than three copies kept.

_record_stalls calls _last_verdict_of(run_id) once per pointer (:1453) and _last_stage_seconds(stage) once per stall (:1491), and each call re-reads and re-parses the entire verdict log (capped at 1 MB); a pass over a queue of N requests therefore does at least 2N full parses of that file on the admission service loop, where one read per pass would serve every lookup.

the drain view compares against the literal "stalled" where the writer defines queue_admission.STALL_VERDICT, so renaming the verdict constant leaves the reader silently matching nothing and every stall clears as if a later verdict had replaced it.

the needs-you row is reachable only from tests in production: nothing under reckon/ imports reckon.crew.needs_you at all — needs_you_rows is called only from needs_you() (:252), needs_you_runs only from needs_you() — so the stall's delivery to a request's session, which the plan names as its route, is exercised only by the test's direct call; the plan chose this module, so this is recorded rather than scored against the node.

the base arm's four failures are all `AttributeError: module 'reckon.crew.queue_admission' has no attribute 'STALL_VERDICT'` raised at tests/test_the_queue_reports_its_own_stalls.py:90 inside the _stalls helper, after admit_once has already returned; the manifest reads that as showing "the behaviour is genuinely new rather than already-correct code reimplemented", but it only shows the constant is new — a base that already recorded stalls perfectly would fail identically, so the reproduction claim is stronger than the log supports.
